newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan protesters may drop trip to disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan protesters may drop trip to disputed isles.

text.p: A Taiwan activist said on Tuesday his group would cancel a planned protest trip to a disputed East China Sea archipelago if Tokyo agreed to stop what he called harassment of Taiwan fishermen in waters near the islands.

Taipei county councilman Chin Chieh-sho said the outcome of talks between Taipei and Tokyo would determine whether his group would try to land on October 6 on the islands now held by Japan, the state-run Central News Agency reported.

The sailing, expected to field more than 20 boats, would be the latest in a wave of anti-Japanese protests to sweep Taiwan and Hong Kong and the first since an activist was killed during a bid by Hong Kong protesters to reach the isles last week.

"If Japan agrees to let Taiwan fishing boats work within 12 nautical miles of the Diaoyu islands or to tear down its lighthouse and flag, I am willing to cancel the October 6 activity immediately," Chin was quoted as saying.

Tensions have run high since July when a Japanese right-wing group built a lighthouse and planted a Japanese flag on the uninhabited islands -- known to Chinese as the Diaoyu and to Japanese as the Senkaku -- to assert Tokyo's sovereignty.
Japan, Taiwan and China all claim the islands.

The tension escalated in August and September when Japanese patrol boats repelled private Taiwanese boats attempting to take protesters, fishermen and journalists to the islands, triggering calls for a more forceful responses from Beijing and Taipei.

Taipei, which has urged calm in the face of growing anti-Japanese anger, has said it expected to hold talks with Tokyo on October 3 or 4 to discuss fishing rights and other issues. Japan has not confirmed the schedule.

The dispute took on new urgency with the September 26 death of Hong Kong activist David Chan, who was killed when he dived into waters near the islands as a protest after his boat too was turned away by Japanese patrols.
Chin said the new protest group would include many trained divers and doctors in order to prevent further fatalities.
Group members on Thursday rehearsed for a possible landing on the Diaoyus by riding rubber rafts and motorcycle-like waverunners in heavy seas near Taiwan's northern Keelung coast.

Japan took the islands northeast of Taiwan as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895. While China and Taiwan claim Japan's ownership is illegal, Tokyo refuses to acknowledge any sovereignty dispute.
China and Taiwan, separated by a civil war in 1949, say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have returned after Japan's World War Two defeat.
